data.content_ref: inline:The target's defense rests on two distinct criteria — 'higher empirical content' and 'has not yet been falsified' — but these criteria cannot combine to yield a non-inductive preference without one doing the other's work. Empirical content is a static logical property of a theory's form (how many possible observations it rules out); it is fixed at the moment of proposal and is entirely unaffected by whether the theory subsequently survives testing. If empirical content alone justified preference, the survival condition would be superfluous: we would prefer the boldest theory regardless of test results. Conversely, if survival of severe tests is what makes the theory 'the best available target for future criticism,' the target must explain why past survival is relevant to future critical worth — which is precisely the inductive move the target denies making. The target's phrase 'a bold theory that survives is more informative than a cautious one' conflates these: boldness (content) is prior to and independent of survival, so survival adds zero informational value on the target's own non-inductive terms. The argument thus contains a structural gap: it invokes two independently insufficient criteria and gives no account of how they jointly produce a non-inductive recommendation, leaving the survival criterion either vacuous (content does all the work) or inductive (survival does all the work).
